utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning to you Mr. Brdjanin. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, sorry about that. I didn't realise it wasn't on. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova, Sureta Chana and Hasan Younis case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman with Brian Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you both. So let's go to private session for a short while because I need to communicate something to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With your kind permission I will now call our next witness, which will be 7.156, Dzevad Doslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he doesn't enjoy any --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any measures so that will be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you, Mr. Doslic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from your reaction, I take it that you are receiving an interpretation of what I am saying in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you. So let's proceed. You are about to start giving evidence and before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be telling us the truth and the whole truth. That's the equivalent of an oath in several jurisdictions. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher to your left is going to hand to you. Your duty is to read that text aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be speaking the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And you may sit down. What's going to happen very briefly is that you are going to be asked a number of questions, first from the Prosecution, and subsequently, and afterwards, by the Defence of Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. Your responsibility is towards justice and towards the truth. You have no right to make a distinction between the Prosecution and the Defence. You have to answer -- your duty is to answer any question irrespective of where it's coming from, as fully and as truthfully as possible, and to the best of your ability. My other suggestion, and advice, to you is that from past experience, witnesses that come over here tend to want to elaborate on the information that is asked from them. That's a mistake. When you are asked a question, try to answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question, because if you move outside the parameters of the question, you might end up in a lot of undesired and undesirable problems. Okay? So the witness is in your hands, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With your kind permission I will lead the witness on his personal particulars. Examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Your name is Dzevad Doslic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on 24th August, 1957; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your ethnic origin is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're a Muslim by religion?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your current occupation is an electrician?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me, did you complete your JNA military service at any time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: 15 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was during your compulsory service, was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where were you employed in 1977?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In Sipad Janj company in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that job?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: You mean before the army or after the army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the army, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: After the army, all the way up to 1989, the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you always a civilian or did you have any political inclinations?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. I was always a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take you to the end of 1991, please? And the beginning of 1992. Where were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: At that time, in the beginning of 1991, I spent a month in Austria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Donji Vakuf at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I had been in Austria only for one month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did you return to Donji Vakuf after being in Austria for a month?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what happened when you did come to Donji Vakuf at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened generally or what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: To him as he walked into the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that clear to you? We are referring you to your return to Donji Vakuf from Austria, and Madam Chana would like to know what happened, as far as you are concerned, upon your return. What did you find? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean in 1991 or in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you returned from Austria to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991, I spent there one month and then I was there again in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's go to 1992. When did you come to Donji Vakuf in 1992 to visit your family?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In 1992, that was in sometime July or August, end July, beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What did you find as you entered Donji Vakuf? Were you allowed to -- free access into Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do when you went there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I came to town, it was a Friday, I was supposed to return on Sunday, and when we got on to the bus at the exit from Donji Vakuf, the Serbian police stopped us and turned us back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the police? How do you know it was the police?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, they had arm bands with Cyrillic writing on it saying the police with the four S sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, I think -- I need to intervene a little bit here because I see that we can potentially be heading towards a lot of confusion here. Sir, you told us that you spent one month in Austria working there in 1991. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When? Which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From June to July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you went back to Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Donji Vakuf before you went back to Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost a year, because in 1992, I went there again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because then he relates events that had took place in May and in June. So almost a year. So you then went to Austria again. Do you remember the month in 1992 when you went to Austria again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which month it was. I know it was the end of spring, the beginning of summer. I can't tell you exactly now because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you told us before that as far as you can remember, you returned to Donji Vakuf in July or August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in 1992, when did you return to Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, it was, I think -- I couldn't tell you the exact month now but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you say you went to Austria towards the end of spring of 1992 and you only spent one month there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When do you think that you returned, then, to Donji Vakuf? April, May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it was the end of April, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that fits in the rest of the statement that he made to you, because otherwise, having told us that he returned to Donji Vakuf in 1992 in July, August, doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can go ahead, at least we know exactly what happened now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's early 1992 that you returned and now you were telling us that you found the police there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: When they stopped us, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You are now in Donji Vakuf going home. You see police. What are these policemen doing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing, I had come thinking that I would only be spending the weekend there, and when we were going back on Sunday, we were stopped by the police, as we were leaving the town, and it turned -- they turned the bus back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At which point were you turned back? Where was it that this bus that were you travelling on --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was at the exit from Donji Vakuf, on the road to Jajce and the bus was going to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who stopped the bus?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: They said we couldn't go on and that we had to go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask the reason why?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't. They only ordered the bus to turn around. The driver of the bus talked to them and he had to make a U-turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you were turned back?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We went back to the bus station and we went our separate ways, all went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere generally in Donji Vakuf at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Every day people would retreat to their own streets, to their own houses. They appeared in greater numbers in the streets at intersections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say people, can you describe who these people are, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: All the citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnicity retreated to their houses and apartments, whereas the Serb population had left town for the most part and some of them were moving around in streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These Serbs which were moving around in streets, can you describe to me whether they were in uniform or in civilian clothes and what they were up to, what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The police was dressed in blue, brown uniforms, whereas soldiers were wearing both drab green olive grey uniforms and camouflage uniforms, and all of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they doing anything else as they were patrolling those streets?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: At that time, that week when I had returned, they were not doing anything in particular but people were still intimidated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims have any uniforms, were they patrolling the street at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you quickly tell me what was the proportion of the population at that time in Donji Vakuf between the Serbs and the Bosniaks and the Croats, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Donji Vakuf, with the surrounding villages, had around 24 or 25.000 people. 65 per cent Muslims, 33 per cent Serbs and 2 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where the Serbs got their weapons from at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask or find out why they were doing what they were doing, why they were armed and patrolling the streets?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't ask, and we couldn't understand what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I take you to the 2nd of May, 1992? Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was on that day that the bridge was blown up. It was the 1st or the 2nd of May. I believe it was the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which bridge is this, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was the bridge across the Vrbas River, linking Donji Vakuf with the road to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you saw this bridge being blown up?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, I passed through a few minutes prior to that, ten minutes or five minutes, I'm not exactly sure, I passed over the bridge and some 300 to 400 metres from the bridge, I saw thick smoke and I heard an explosion, very loud one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in the morning or the afternoon, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you with at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I was with my wife and children at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there many other people on that bridge on that particular day at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, since the situation was tense, there were few people moving about, but there were several people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you sort of roughly guess estimate as to how many civilians would be on that bridge?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, after about an hour or two, as my mother, father and sister live in the vicinity of the bridge, I passed through the area and I saw three to four corpses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you said earlier that you heard a blast as you were 200 metres away from the bridge. Did you look behind at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I saw a thick black smoke and I saw that in downtown, roof tiles had fallen off roofs, in the downtown area. I saw window panes broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do thereafter?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: After about an hour or two, as my father, mother and sister lived Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the vicinity, I wanted to see them and passing through the area, I saw two to three bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who they were? Or did you subsequently find out who they were?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We found that out after about an hour or two, I'm not sure exactly how long. There was an old barber there whom all of us knew because it was a small town. Then there was a waiter and a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit your mother on that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to your mother?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Since she was some 100 to 150 metres away, she was sitting, and a large wardrobe fell on her, on her head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This wardrobe that fell on her head, was it as a result of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because the windows and the doors were all shook by the detonation. The windows were broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened after this explosion? What was the atmosphere in Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The entire downtown area was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way was it destroyed, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Roof tiles had fallen off roofs. The windows of the shops were broken. The house that was by the bridge where there was a coffee bar completely disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the people of Donji Vakuf? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: People in Donji Vakuf withdrew, went back to their homes and apartments. They didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, what did they do next?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. People stayed in their houses. They ventured out very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they all remain in Donji Vakuf or did they start leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: When the bridge was blown up, from that day on, people started leaving the town in waves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "people," what ethnic origins were they who were leaving in waves?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims at that point arm themselves?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who actually went and got a weapon to protect themselves?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, I had a relative who had a weapon, and he dug it into the soil and left town. He was a butcher. He had a permit to carry a pistol. He also bought an automatic rifle and when people started leaving town, he buried it into sand and went to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court his name, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Esad Saleta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, there were -- the Muslims were not arming themselves at this time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- did you have a neighbour by the name of Celic Halil?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about him, please? What was he doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: At that time, when the Serb police and troops were moving in the area, he used to point out in which houses there were Muslims who had remained there, and he went with them from one street to the next one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now, how many Muslims remained in the town after this mass exodus, as it were, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, after the bridge, people started leaving in waves but approximately at least half of the Muslim and Croatian population remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you suggest some figures to this Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you figures, but as far as I know, definitely one half remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your own reason for remaining in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally wasn't aware of the gravity of the situation. It didn't occur to me that things could happen, the things that later came to pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now take to you 16th June, 1992, sir? Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell this Court, please, what happened on that date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: That was the day of our holiday, Kurban Bajram. They came to my house, together with Halil Celic. My sister came out. They were looking for me. And they said to her, should I fail to report to them, that they would take my entire family to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Halil Celic came. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: My sister saw him, and I saw him later on, when I started out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any reason given at the time as to why they needed to see you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No, no. They simply said I should report to SUP, since I live in the centre of the town that was some 300 to 400 metres away, or rather I should have said MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to MUP?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then arrested or you reported to MUP yourself?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Since in their car they had some other people whom I didn't know, they told me to report to MUP and should I not do that, they would take my entire family to Manjaca. That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other persons they arrested on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Abdulah Began, Esad Becar, Fahrudin Plivcic, Nasko Doslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- you said then you reported to MUP. And what did you tell your family before you went?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I said to my father, "Try to get the remaining ones out of here, if you can. I'm leaving."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you walked to the MUP, what did -- were the streets crowded or deserted or what did you find?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The streets were empty. Muslim houses had been broken into. Items were carried out of those houses. There were things strewn in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these people who were carrying out these items?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: All of those people were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they civilians, were they soldiers, and how did you know which one they were?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Since that was a small town, almost all of us knew each other. Those were Serb policemen, troops, women, children, civilians, all of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know -- what uniforms were these Serbian soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The police uniforms were blue and brown. Military uniforms were camouflage uniforms and the former JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened when you went to MUP then?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Ten metres before the MUP building, two guys came out with automatic rifles. One grabbed me by one arm, the other took my other arm, and they took me into the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take your belongings at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, when we got in, they took everything we had on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they and what ethnic origins were they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In the hallway, I saw about a dozen people. Those were Muslims. Among them I recognised Mustafa Ceric, and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened to you when you were inside? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you're in MUP and you've been frisked, what happens next to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, we stood there in the hallway for some three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Then after that, they opened up the warehouse of the Territorial Defence, which was in the vicinity of MUP. They took us there, opened the door and as they opened the door, we saw that there were some other people there and they locked us in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will at this stage, Your Honour, show him some photographs and then if he can recognise -- sorry, Your Honour. Photographs from P1706 -- sorry, Your Honour can I come again? P1760.6 to .21. If he can be handed all these photographs by the usher, then he can identify them as he goes along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Doslic, the usher is bringing you some photographs, if you could please look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you hand the photographs to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the other camp called Vrbaspromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can look through the photographs, sir, and when you identify the warehouse, then you can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Usher if you could please assist. If you could let him have the photographs, he can look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look through these photographs sir and when you do come to that, just look through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] For the time being he's just going to have a look at them, he's going to give an information on each and every one, we need to specify what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, no, if he can now put that picture on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, we are showing you now Exhibit P1760.15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What do you see in that picture?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: This is the warehouse, the warehouse above the MUP building where they locked us in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, 25 to 30 metres approximately. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything else in this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: This used to be the TO warehouse. The first door behind the first door is where they kept us, and behind the second door, there was a division made of metal, and they kept military equipment there, blankets, things like that. We were not allowed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at photograph P1760.11, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you see in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: This was the other warehouse belonging to Vrbaspromet. We were kept there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to them. Sorry. Was there anything in this warehouse? What was inside it except the people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. It was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell us how many people there were in this warehouse when you were incarcerated in it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In the first one or in the second one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about 95 of us, 97. I couldn't tell you but around that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in this particular warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In the first one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the first one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you the exact date, because I don't remember, but perhaps some 20 days, if not more, and then after that, we were transferred to this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a minute so if you can go back to the first warehouse, can you tell us the conditions that you were kept in?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a warehouse constructed out of steel frame and the floor was made out of concrete. We had to lie along one wall or the other wall in the warehouse. The middle area had to be vacant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given food?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to take baths?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: There was no water there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We had a bucket about this big.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit P1760.15, please, if that can be put on the ELMO? .15, yes. Is that the warehouse from the outside?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: This is the TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, which we are now talking about. We just want to be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: That was where we were imprisoned the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten in this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see others beaten in this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, very often, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would beat them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would they beat them? In the warehouse or outside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, first they would call out the person to come out. Then they would close the door and then some three to four of them would come, beat the person up, and then bring him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they always beat people outside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. Some people were scared so much that they wouldn't come out, thinking they wouldn't touch them if they were there, and then they would beat the person in front of all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us any one that you particularly remember who got beaten?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, they would beat somebody called Pajic, who was a forester very often. They would most frequently take him down to the garage. They also beat Mustafa Ceric. There was a teacher there who long time before that gave a failing grade to a Serb student, and the teacher now had to wait for him every day in order to kiss his shoes and then the Serb man would beat him, hit him, do all kinds of things to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any resistance whatsoever from the Muslim detainees when they were beaten? Were they in a position to resist?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen to the injured people after they had been beaten? Were they provided with medical care and attention?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some names of Serb soldiers who you said used to beat these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Nenad Svemir, Jordan Ilic, Sasa Krivosija, a person named Balaban, then Stojan Subasic. They were the most ferocious ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know these people how? How do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, Stojan Subasic used to work with me. The others that I named are people I know because I know everyone in this small town. Everybody knows everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew them before and you recognised them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe the state of the injuries that you would find on these prisoners after they'd been beaten up, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the nephew of my wife, Safet Omerovic, he was 80 years old. His back was so badly beaten that he couldn't even walk. Other people were also badly injured. Some more, some less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they would pick out certain people to be beaten and not others?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether it is silver lining or what, luck, in a general misfortune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who died as a result of these beatings in that particular warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In this warehouse? No. But in the other one, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever overhear a conversation while in this first warehouse, between two Serb soldiers about certain people being killed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever overhear a conversation between some Serb guards over some people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We overheard them talking amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, they were saying that across the road from this warehouse, there is a small settlement, that's where they brought out Suljo Softic, a 70 year old man. They killed him. Also next to his house, they killed Haka Omeragic, and three houses down, there lived a barber, an old barber, Jusuf. They brought him outside the MUP building, and I must say that MUP and the warehouse are ten metres apart, and through this window, we could see through a small hole, when they brought Jusuf. They brought him outside the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Jusuf? Did you see what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We could see through that window when it happened. This Haka Omeragic is Jusuf's brother. When he saw Jusuf being killed, he had been brought outside the MUP and he cursed their Chetnik mother, and the Serbs were 20 or 30 in that group. All of them came down very hard on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise some of the Serb soldiers with this group of 15 to 20? Can you give us some names that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. For example, Nenad Svemir, Vojo Ilic, Jordan Ilic. There were others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all in Serbian uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he die then, Jusuf Omeragic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the camp commander was where you were detained in this warehouse, the commander of that particular camp?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Miodrag or Milorad Djurkic. Any way, I know the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you think he was the guard, the camp guard, the camp commander, rather, sorry?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, when we had been released from the previous camp to do our work obligation, we saw on the papers we received that he was the manager or commander of that prison, whatever you want to call him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him yourself at the time you were there, this commander Djurkic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In that other camp, he had an office in Vrbaspromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what -- you said you were detained there about 20 days or so; is that correct, in this TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would bring you to about early July, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was sometime around the 20th or the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next to you? Where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: After that, there came a freight truck covered by a tarpaulin. This first door opened. Three or four policemen came in and told us, "When we call somebody's name out, they should step out." And they started calling out names, and they tied people's hands and blindfolded them and put them on to this truck. When they had loaded everyone in, they told them that they were going to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yourself? Were you one of them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. Those of us who remained were picked up the next day by a small TAM truck without a tarpaulin, an open truck, and we were taken in three or four groups to a warehouse of Vrbaspromet company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you taken there? How many of you, sorry, were there in this truck that went to this Vrbaspromet warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was a small truck and we were packed in, 10, 15 or 20 at a time, and we had to lie down. We were forbidden to look either way. Up Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there, next to the truck cab, a Serb policeman was standing with an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at Exhibit P1760.5, if that could be placed on the ELMO, please? Thank you. Is this picture -- do you recognise this? Is this where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next one, .6, please? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see .7, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: .8, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And .11, please, usher, that's the inside, .11, that's three photographs down. Now, is this the inside of that particular warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It is, only then it was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was empty? There was nothing in it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Right. There was nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big a space was this, to your estimation, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 30 metres in length by 20, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got there, were there people already there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were they?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: As we were filing in, I was in the last group, there might have been 30 or 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Altogether, how many people were in this particular warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We were about 90, 95, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now describe to the Court, please, the conditions in this warehouse, the conditions under which you lived?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The warehouse was empty at the time. The floor was concrete, and there were only wooden pallets to sit on and lie on. We had no water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food? What kind of food were you given?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We got, for instance, five -- 400 to 500 gram loaf per 50 men, sometimes once a day, sometimes once in three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was this warehouse guarded by?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: They changed all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the personalities changed but were they all from certain police force?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of these guards?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I knew 95 per cent of them. For some of them I knew the first name or the last name. I told you already it was a small place. We all knew each other. For instance, there was Lazo Boroja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commander of this particular warehouse was?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The commander?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: You mean of the prison?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, this --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Djurkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you notice the condition of the people when you entered this warehouse? What was the general condition of the other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Their condition was worse because they had been brought earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "worse" sir, could you please describe to us what they looked like? Did they have injuries? Were they dirty? What was the general demeanour of these people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, they had lost weight. Some of them were beaten up. They were generally filthy and disheveled. There were no conditions for personal hygiene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there one particular person that you saw there which was particularly badly wounded?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Ljuban Mrsic, an older man, a shepherd. He was taken in before we were, while he would still talk he told us they had taken his sheep away and brought him there. He was so badly beaten up that his spine and this part here was broken, and he had maggots on his back. Worms were crawling on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these would be from his wounds; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his condition apparent to the -- his captors?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone who came in had to feel the stench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they provide you with any medical aid or assistance or any of these people in that particular room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Ljuban Mrsic then?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, he suffered for about 15 days, and then one day, in the small hours, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other persons who died in this particular warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also an older man by the name of Mehdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see two of your neighbours arrive at this camp?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about them and who they were and what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was a neighbour of mine, Mahmut Omeragic and another neighbour Midhat Softic, also known as Mica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, they were brought in. Mica was in a very bad state, and Mahmut wasn't. They spent the night there and the next day, sometime in the afternoon, a Serb soldier came for them, a man named Tanasic, nicknamed Tana. He had a green pickup truck. He tied their hands and blindfolded them and told them that they were going to be exchanged. Nobody has heard of them since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this be around the 22nd of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Around that time. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any minors in this camp, this - I'm sorry I do not pronounce it properly - Vrbaspromet camp? Were there any minors there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two minors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their ages, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid to get it wrong but they could have been 13, 14, certainly not more than 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of all the soldiers which would come to this camp, who amongst them you thought were the most brutal that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The most brutal man, I told you already, both in the first and the second camp, the most brutal men were those I had already enumerated. If you want me, I can tell you their names again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would be so kind to do so.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: All those who were in the first camp, who I named as the most brutal were also in the second camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw them at both camps? That's the important point I want the Court to understand.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And amongst them was Svemir and Ilic, right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. They are two separate men, Svemir is one man, Jordan Ilic is the second man. There is the third man Krivosija, there was also Vojo Ilic, then Balaban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, can we take you to 23rd of July, 1992? Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us what happened then on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Ceric, Muharem Teskeregic and I were called into the office of Miodrag Djurkic, and he told us that he was releasing us to do our work obligation. Since the town was abandoned, my family, my wife and children had remained, whereas many other people had left, and the wives of Mustafa Ceric and Muharem also remained at the time when we were released to do the work obligation. Several days later, they also released Nasko Doslic, Selim Hamdija. At any rate, there were seven or eight of us who were released to do our work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said your work obligation, what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: That implied that you had to go to work somewhere. If you allow me, I will quote one example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: For instance, I was forced to slaughter cows and cattle for them in the slaughterhouse that belonged to a relative of mine. Mustafa Ceric, a man who used to be a director of a company, was forced to sweep the road, carry out garbage, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your assignment, your work assignment?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: My work assignments implied that I was taken to work by Boroja, Lazo Boroja, and I was brought back after working for five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you worked for Boroja. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No. It was Novo Boroja. He was the man who took me out and brought me back. Novo Boroja was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the slaughterhouse that you worked for six hours a day?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was a slaughterhouse along the road to Jajce, about three kilometres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you continue this work detail of yours?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on the 23rd of December?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of December, this man came. I think it was Novo Boroja, and he said that it was announced over the radio that 13 of us Muslims, including two of my young daughters, were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this mean, that you were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, that meant that 13 of us were later exchanged for 39 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Chana, I think we need to stop here for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break and we will resume immediately after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to continue, Mr. Doslic before the break, you were telling us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, before the break, Mr. Doslic, you were telling this Court that from 24th July, until your exchange on 25th -- 23rd of December, you were on this work detail in the slaughterhouse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you, Mr. Doslic, to tell this Court, during this time, that is 24th July, to 23rd December, you remain in the town of Donji Vakuf and some of the incidents which happened during those months. Can you first tell this Court, please, what was the atmosphere in Donji Vakuf at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: At that time, from the moment when we came to perform our work obligation, there were perhaps only some 30 to 40 Muslim residents in the entire town, including men, women and children. All of the Muslim houses were torn apart. Items were being carried out from those houses, loaded up on vehicles and so on. There were property items strewn in the streets, backyards, everywhere, but all of the Muslim houses had been broken into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these people who were carrying off these looted goods, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: They were Serb soldiers, policemen, Serb civilians, women, children, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you nearly stabbed once? Or nearly stabbed, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, one day, we went to load up hay in a village. Novo Boroja was with me. I was loading up the hay, as was he, and at one moment, I turned around and I saw an elderly woman, a Serb lady, called Andja. She had a sabre or a long knife, this big, and Novo managed to put himself between the two of us. Then she said, "Are there any balijas around, remaining? Fuck their mothers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you happen to go into your own house at this time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: After the work obligation, I had to go to my house, which had also been broken into. Things were thrown around, some things had been carried out, some hadn't. Novo Boroja used to come every morning to fetch me and then in the evening he would bring me back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your family still living in Donji Vakuf in your house?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: All of my family members left Donji Vakuf when the others did. Only my wife and two little daughters remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was life like for them during this period, Mr. Doslic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was no life at all. Children didn't dare go into the backyard. They had to stay shut in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they provide for their basic essentials?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Since we were living in the house, in our house, in which my brother and my aunt had lived before leaving town, there were a lot of food items there. Later on, I have to say that Novo Boroja helped us a lot. He helped us a great deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see yourself these goods being loaded into vehicles and being taken away from Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. A military vehicle would come, a large one, with a tarpaulin, and it would go door-to-door, house to house, and collect what they liked. Later on, they would drive towards the slaughterhouse. There was a Muslim weekend cottage there, and there was a large field there, and some kind of a military base of theirs was located there. They warehoused the goods that they liked in that location, and then if, later on, whenever they needed to go to Banja Luka or elsewhere, perhaps to Serbia, they would drive the goods there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw that personally, did you, the driving away, I mean?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large field there. On one side was the slaughterhouse, and running in the middle of it was the main road to Jajce and this is where they were. The field was crowded with goods. I would also see them when they came into the street. They would go door-to-door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Doslic. Now I'd like to take you to the summer of 1992. Do you know a mosque called Dudica Dzamija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should team up with Ms. Korner in your pronunciation, you are in competition.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to learn the language, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know, it's called Dudica Dzamija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now what do you know about this mosque, firstly, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was a mosque situated on the main road leading from Jajce to Travnik, to Sarajevo. It was in town. It was built of wood. The building and the minarets and the rest of it was built of solid construction material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this mosque, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it happen that you saw this fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a small town, and the part that was built of wood was quite old and one could see the smoke very well, and whenever they came, they would talk about it, and let me stress once again, Novo Boroja truly helped me a lot, and he confirmed this to me as well, and I saw the smoke myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it that Novo Boroja confirmed to you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Novo Boroja prompted by my question about the smoke, told me that the mosque had been set on fire, and some two or three days later, I went with Novo Boroja and passed through the area because I had built a new house for myself in that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw the ruins of this mosque?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It was still smouldering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this Court, please, if you know, who started this fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever informed as to this fire and the cause of it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, we learned that either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers had set it on fire. It definitely wasn't the Muslims who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Doslic, I will take you to August of 1992. Do you remember that you also witnessed a bridge being blown up at this time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- sorry, I'll take that question back, Your Honours, if I may, and ask him about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that a line -- page 37, line 17, where the transcript says "we learned," that what the witness actually said was, "we thought that either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers had set it on fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it does. Mr. Doslic, Mr. Doslic, you have heard what Mr. Ackerman has just pointed out to us. What did you actually say earlier on? You were asked the following question: Were you ever informed as to this fire, and the cause of it? And our transcript says, "Well," according to you, "we learned that either Serb policemen or Serb soldiers had set it on fire." Did you say, "we learned" or "we thought" -- "we believed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We learned, we learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour I think the witness also continued to say it was not the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's important at this point is whether they learned or whether they thought or figured it out. And he's confirming that he said that they learned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I was just pointing out the transcript does not reflect that additional sentence. But be that as it may, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know another mosque called Bas-Dzamija?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that located, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: It is in the centre of the town, 300 metres from my house, 300 to 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what happened to this particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Well, one day, I don't remember exactly what time it was, but in the morning hours, there was a very loud explosion so that once again the downtown area was affected again, even though it had been ruined prior to that. A similar explosion took place like the one that had taken place at the bridge. Since I was working at the slaughterhouse, Novo and I would, from time to time, come to the downtown area to deliver meat, and then I saw that the mosque had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see at the site of the destroyed mosque? What was happening to the rubble?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: They brought in bulldozers and trucks and loaded up remains on them and threw them into the Vrbas River or some of it was thrown next to the river and some of it into the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ground where the mosque was, what was its condition at the end of all of this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: At the end, they razed it nicely, and then they put sand there and turned it into a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you still see remains of this mosque in the Vrbas River today, if one was to look?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could, and next to the river as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also know a mosque called Fadilova Dzamija? Once again, I apologise for my pronunciation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Fadilova's mosque. Yes, I know that's close to Dudica Dzamija. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dudica Dzamija and Fadilova's Dzamija are about 100 to 200 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The same. It had been set on fire and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this particular mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Dudica mosque and Fadilova's mosque were destroyed in a matter of two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see the ruins of this particular mosque, yourself?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've told you that these two mosques are close to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to confirm that you saw them yourself, the ruins?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, on 22nd of December, 1992, do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of December?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd or 23rd was when we were exchanged. They told us to get ready to take just our clothing with us, that we were not allowed to take watches or gold with us and they told us we were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've already indicated to this Court earlier in your testimony that you were exchanged on the 23rd of December but on the 22nd of December, how did you learn that you were to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Since we had no access to the media, to the radio, we were not allowed to have radio stations in our house, Boro -- Novo Boroja told us that there might be an exchange the following day but that he wasn't sure about that and he told me that if I wished, I could go into the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, informed you of this exchange?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The following day, a short man, or rather a Serb neighbour of ours, came, a boy who was 12 or 13 years old and he said that he had been sent by Novo, who couldn't come himself, to inform us to get ready and to go to the bus station at 11.00. He said that all 13 of us would come there and that we were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where, in fact were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: We were exchanged halfway between Donji Vakuf and another place, there was a farm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name of the particular village? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: The name of the place is Kopcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, who else other than yourself and your family of course was present during this exchange?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: You mean the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Serb, if any Serb officials.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Nikola Kisin there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Nikola Kisin?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Nikola Kisin was my teacher, my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was an official as well?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: He was president of the SDS in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Muslims were exchanged for how many Serbs, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: There were 13 of us Muslims, including my two girls, and we were exchanged for 39 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than Nikola Kisin, the SDS president, which other Serbs were present during this exchange? Other than the prisoners, of course.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: There were three or four soldiers escorting him. There was another man from the other part of town. We called him Slipko I don't know his real name. And this other man, I know, but I don't know his name. And on the side that greeted us, there was representative of the HVO called Soldo, I don't know his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after the exchange?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: After the exchange I went towards Bugojno. When I came to Bugojno, since my neighbours were there, I inquired about my parents, and they told me that my parents were in Gornji Vakuf, so I headed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever meet your fellow camp detainees at some point in -- after you were released, after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you met and what information was passed to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Immediately on the following day, there in the vicinity, I saw Safet Omeragic, my wife's uncle, who had been imprisoned as well. Then I saw some 30 per cent of those who had been imprisoned with me. I saw them in the course of the following seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what information did they give to you about fellow detainees having been killed?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: For example, Safet, my wife's uncle, told me that when they were exchanged in Turbe, that just before the exchange, a Serb soldier came and said that two of the youngest should be taken out. Among them -- the two of them were called Saban and Spaho. When they got off the truck, the Serb soldier kill them because allegedly his son had been killed and he wanted to take revenge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then remain in Bugojno until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you join the BiH Army in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: In April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Doslic, I'm going to show you some documents with the Court's permission and I would like you to just look at them. The first document I would like to show you is 7.156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you've got it wrong, Madam Chana. 7.156 is -- yes, exactly, it refers to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the witness number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right. The first document Your Honour is P1703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour this is not on the list that was given me so I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have it either. I have 1702 and 1705. But 1703 and 4 are not listed. However, let's see what it is first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to be able to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes me too exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's a very short document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the -- I see. All right. Let's have a look at least at it. Put it on the ELMO in the English version. Yes, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dated 13th January, 1992, and it's a Serbian Democratic Party of BH, Donji Vakuf, SDS municipal board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the names from one to seven therein?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you put the names there, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: As I've told you, Nedeljko Ninkovic was also my teach ever as was Nikola Kisin. I know Nikica Zagorac, Miodrag Jandric was a Judge and an attorney. I know Zeljko Nenad as well. Ljubo Mekinjic used to work at the municipality and I know Zoran Glisic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the Nikola Kisin who was present at your exchange? Is it the same name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD DOSLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Nikola Kisin was present during my exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The next document, Your Honour -- if you'll bear with me, Your Honour -- is Exhibit P1705, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Serbian Municipality of Donji Vakuf, where it established the seat of the municipality in Donji Vakuf, and it gives the area of the Serbian Municipality of Donji Vakuf shall comprise of the following localities.
